sections.heading: 2.4 WHO meeting in Geneva to review the situation (22–23 Jan)
sections.summary: As Wuhan locks down and China admits human-to-human transmission, a WHO Geneva meeting on 22–23 Jan fails to agree on declaring a PHEIC.

sections.heading: 2.5 No PHEIC declared — Farrar contacts Fauci (23 Jan)

sections.heading: 2.6 Global Preparedness Monitoring Board steps in (27–28 Jan)
sections.summary: The GPMB (with Farrar and Fauci as board members) circulates a draft statement still praising China's ‘transparency’ and ‘collaboration’, even as WHO staff privately fume over stonewalling.

sections.title: Dr. Tedros is in Beijing to try to negotiate WHO access (end Jan)
sections.heading: 2.7 Dr. Tedros is in Beijing to try to negotiate WHO access (end Jan)

sections.title: Tedros praises China further back in Geneva (29 Jan)
sections.heading: 2.8 Tedros praises China further back in Geneva (29 Jan)

evidence.raw: China Daily: page 1 and page 2 (with infographics)

sections.heading: 2.9 WHO reaches out to Fauci, Farrar and Redfield (29–30 Jan)
sections.summary: WHO's Michael Ryan loops in Fauci, Farrar and Redfield for an informal chat with Tedros; Farrar separately asks Fauci for his personal views on the virus's origin.

sections.title: Dr. Tedros praises China while declaring a Health Emergency (30 Jan)
sections.heading: 2.10 Dr. Tedros praises China while declaring a Health Emergency (30 Jan)

sections.summary: The first press mentions of a possible lab origin (Daily Mail, Washington Times, Washington Post) appear and are quickly dismissed; Sen. Cotton raises the question politically, while Trump keeps praising China for trade reasons.

sections.title: Baric lays out some concerns (29 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.2 Baric lays out some concerns (29 Jan)
sections.summary: Baric later testifies he laid out three possible origins — natural, lab escape of a natural virus, or lab escape of an engineered one — at a classified BSEG meeting, though newly released documents suggest the actual date was 29 Jan.

sections.title: Farrar learns about some US scientist doubts (before 27 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.3 Farrar learns about some US scientist doubts (before 27 Jan)
sections.summary: Farrar learns, via unnamed ‘credible scientists’ in the US, that the virus looks ‘almost engineered to infect human cells’ — most likely relayed through his MI5 contacts rather than directly from the scientists themselves.

sections.title: Farrar gets some advice from MI5 (27 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.4 Farrar gets some advice from MI5 (27 Jan)

evidence.raw: Jeremy Farrar, as recorded in his book, Spike

sections.summary: Farrar consults former MI5 chief Eliza Manningham-Buller and requests a burner phone the same day — Andersen later says he believes the original rumours came from UK intelligence.

sections.title: Farrar talks to Holmes on his new burner phone (27 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.5 Farrar talks to Holmes on his new burner phone (27 Jan)
sections.summary: On his new burner phone, Farrar asks Holmes to check whether the virus could be a lab escape; Holmes looks at the data and sees nothing suspicious.

sections.title: Farrar and Vallance talk to Fauci (30 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.6 Farrar and Vallance talk to Fauci (30 Jan)
sections.summary: Farrar and UK chief scientific adviser Vallance hold a short call with Fauci whose purpose is unclear — Fauci later says under oath he has no memory of it.

sections.title: Andersen is independently asked to check the sequence (30 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.7 Andersen is independently asked to check the sequence (30 Jan)
sections.summary: Andersen is separately asked to examine the genome, unaware yet of Holmes's own look days earlier.

sections.title: Andersen expresses his concerns to Holmes (31 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.8 Andersen expresses his concerns to Holmes (31 Jan)
sections.summary: Andersen calls Holmes and flags three red flags in the genome: a near-perfect RBD, a furin cleavage site in a key spot, and the fact that the WIV had been doing exactly this kind of spike/RBD manipulation.

sections.title: Holmes feeds the info back to his ‘handler’ (31 Jan)
sections.heading: 3.9 Holmes feeds the info back to his ‘handler’ (31 Jan)
sections.summary: Holmes tells Andersen he needs to check with his ‘handler’ before going further — Andersen later testifies this confirms Farrar was operating under instruction from UK intelligence.

sections.title: Garry joins Andersen and Holmes — Farrar updates Fauci (31 Jan, ~6 pm EST)
sections.heading: 3.10 Garry joins Andersen and Holmes — Farrar updates Fauci (31 Jan, ~6 pm EST)
sections.summary: Farrar briefs Fauci on Andersen's concerns and sends him profiles of Andersen, Garry and Holmes as the scientists involved, asking Fauci to call Andersen directly.

sections.title: Andersen briefs Fauci (31 Jan, ~7 pm EST)
sections.heading: 3.11 Andersen briefs Fauci (31 Jan, ~7 pm EST)
sections.summary: Andersen walks Fauci through the furin cleavage site, the RBD and other oddities; Fauci suggests going public with a paper, but Andersen says it's too early and more analysis is needed.

sections.title: Fauci suggest a call with a larger group of experts (31 Jan, 7:38 pm EST)
sections.heading: 3.12 Fauci suggest a call with a larger group of experts (31 Jan, 7:38 pm EST)
sections.summary: Fauci proposes widening the review to a larger group of scientists (the future ‘Tony Call’ group) and warns that if Andersen's concerns hold up, the FBI and MI5 would need to be alerted.

sections.title: Constitution of the ‘bounce-off’ group (31 Jan–1 Feb morning)
sections.heading: 3.13 Constitution of the ‘bounce-off’ group (31 Jan–1 Feb morning)
sections.summary: Farrar splits the review into an ‘inner group’ (Holmes, Andersen, Garry, Rambaut — the eventual co-authors) and a separate ‘bounce-off’ group (Fouchier, Drosten, Koopmans, Farzan) to satisfy Fauci's request while keeping the core discussion tight; Baric and Daszak are deliberately excluded for having co-published with the WIV.

sections.title: Fauci shares Cohen’s latest article with Farrar and Andersen (31 Jan, 8:47 pm EST)
sections.heading: 3.14 Fauci shares Cohen’s latest article with Farrar and Andersen (31 Jan, 8:47 pm EST)
sections.summary: Fauci forwards a Science article on the genome's clues to Farrar and Andersen; the piece also carries Daszak's public dismissal of Ebright's lab-origin conjecture.

sections.title: The Farrar call
sections.heading: 4. The Farrar call
sections.summary: Sets up the first full expert review call that Farrar convenes on 1 Feb to assess Andersen's concerns.

sections.title: Information about EHA work with WIV received by Fauci by 31 Jan
sections.heading: 4.1 Information about EHA work with WIV received by Fauci by 31 Jan
sections.summary: NIH staff scramble from 23 Jan to brief Fauci on NIH-funded EcoHealth Alliance/WIV work, flagging Daszak's R01 grant with Baric as a collaborator.

sections.title: Fauci asks his right hand to do some checks (1 Feb, 00:29 am)
sections.heading: 4.2 Fauci asks his right hand to do some checks (1 Feb, 00:29 am)

Fauci’s email to Auchincloss, 1 Feb (half past midnight) (source not clear)

sections.summary: Just after midnight, Fauci tells his deputy Auchincloss to drop everything and check the scope of NIH's funding relationship with China — Fauci later says this was the first he'd heard of it.

sections.title: Farrar sets up the call (1 Feb, 10:34 am EST)
sections.heading: 4.3 Farrar sets up the call (1 Feb, 10:34 am EST)

evidence.raw: People invited to the Farrar call, or included in the follow-up e-mail by Farrar

sections.summary: Farrar formally invites the ‘core’ and ‘bounce-off’ groups to a 2pm call; later testimony confirms Tabak and Collins also joined, while whether Baric was quietly on the line at all remains unresolved.

sections.title: Fauci gets some feedback from Auchincloss (11:47 am EST)
sections.heading: 4.4 Fauci gets some feedback from Auchincloss (11:47 am EST)
sections.summary: Auchincloss reports back that Daszak's grant never needed the extra P3CO review for risky pathogen work — raising the separate question of whether that oversight framework was actually functioning.

sections.title: Andersen sets up a Slack channel to discuss the analysis (1 Feb, 12:11 pm EST)
sections.heading: 4.5 Andersen sets up a Slack channel to discuss the analysis (1 Feb, 12:11 pm EST)
sections.summary: Andersen creates the ‘project-wuhan_engineering’ Slack channel ahead of the call; Holmes previews that the lab-escape idea came from unnamed ‘others’ that Farrar had asked him to look into.

sections.title: Farrar forwards the presentation ahead of the call (1 Feb, 1.12 pm EST)
sections.heading: 4.6 Farrar forwards the presentation ahead of the call (1 Feb, 1.12 pm EST)

evidence.raw: extract of the presentation for the call (‘Coronavirus sequence comparison[1].pdf’), extracted from farrar-fauci-comms-full.pdf

sections.summary: Farrar circulates Rambaut/Andersen/Holmes's sequence-comparison slides, built around six Baric papers on exactly this kind of spike/RBD engineering — with Baric himself excluded from the call over his WIV ties.

sections.title: ‘Derision down the phone line’ (1 Feb, call: 2 to 3 pm EST)
sections.heading: 4.7 ‘Derision down the phone line’ (1 Feb, call: 2 to 3 pm EST)
sections.summary: The call turns into open conflict: Fouchier and Drosten dismiss any engineering discussion outright, leaving the group unable to agree and concluding the question needs a broader, more formal international process.

sections.title: Fauci and Collins suggest publishing (1 Feb, call: 2 to 3 pm EST)
sections.heading: 4.8 Fauci and Collins suggest publishing (1 Feb, call: 2 to 3 pm EST)
sections.summary: Fauci, backed by Collins, suggests the core group write up their doubts as a peer-reviewed paper — premature at this stage, though a confidential report instead would make sense.

sections.title: The core-group ‘After-Call’: ~3 pm to max 4 pm EST
sections.heading: 4.9 The core-group ‘After-Call’: ~3 pm to max 4 pm EST

evidence.raw: Proximal_Origin_Slack.pdf, p.4, 1 Feb 2020, during the call

sections.summary: Andersen, Holmes and Rambaut hold their own private follow-up call, after which Andersen shares the first draft summary of their analysis on Slack.

sections.title: The bosses ‘After-Call’: 3 pm, for probably 10–15 minutes
sections.heading: 4.10 The bosses ‘After-Call’: 3 pm, for probably 10–15 minutes
sections.summary: Farrar, Fauci, Collins, Vallance and Ferguson hold a short closed-door call of their own to agree next steps — Fauci later says he has no memory of it either.

sections.title: Farrar proposes a way out via the WHO (1 Feb, 3:59 pm EST)
sections.heading: 4.11 Farrar proposes a way out via the WHO (1 Feb, 3:59 pm EST)
sections.summary: Farrar writes up a plan to hand the origin question to the WHO using carefully neutral wording, with no mention of Fauci's earlier suggestion to publish a paper.

sections.title: Fauci gets back to the HHS group (1 Feb, ~6 pm EST)
sections.heading: 4.12 Fauci gets back to the HHS group (1 Feb, ~6 pm EST)

evidence.raw: email from 1 Feb 2020 (UK Time), Source: COVID Select Committee tweet

sections.summary: Fauci briefs a group of HHS officials on the call's outcome, repeating Farrar's neutral framing (typo and all) and noting Farrar and Collins will approach Tedros the next day.

sections.title: Grigsby mentions high-level discussions between HHS and WHO (1 Feb, 2:29 pm)
sections.heading: 4.13 Grigsby mentions high-level discussions between HHS and WHO (1 Feb, 2:29 pm)
sections.summary: An HHS email shows Fauci's contacts had already been discussing routing the origin question to the WHO before the Farrar call even happened.

sections.title: US-UK-AU Intel services are informed of the suspicions (after call)
sections.heading: 4.14 US-UK-AU Intel services are informed of the suspicions (after call)
sections.summary: Per Spike, the US, UK and Australian intelligence services are briefed on Andersen's findings after the call — Vallance, Holmes and Collins each updating their own country's services.

sections.title: Farrar and the ‘core-group’ compare notes and estimates
sections.heading: 5. Farrar and the ‘core-group’ compare notes and estimates
sections.summary: Sets up the core group's post-call exchange of probability estimates for a lab-related origin.

sections.title: The FCS can still be explained by passaging (1–2 Feb)
sections.heading: 5.1 The FCS can still be explained by passaging (1–2 Feb)
sections.summary: Despite Fouchier and Drosten's pushback, Farzan and Garry's updated estimates (Farzan: 60:40 to 70:30 for a lab accident) show passaging remains a live hypothesis.

sections.title: Fouchier argues against bothering the WHO with the question (2 Feb, 8:30am UK)
sections.heading: 5.2 Fouchier argues against bothering the WHO with the question (2 Feb, 8:30am UK)
sections.summary: Fouchier argues the question shouldn't go beyond the closed group at all unless a non-natural origin can be shown ‘beyond reasonable doubt’, warning it would otherwise harm science and China.

sections.title: Farrar politely dismisses Fouchier’s concerns to the ‘core group’ (2 Feb, 8:40am UK)
sections.heading: 5.3 Farrar politely dismisses Fouchier’s concerns to the ‘core group’ (2 Feb, 8:40am UK)
sections.summary: Farrar pushes back, arguing it's better to address the question openly now than let it fester and polarise later.

sections.title: Rambaut pushes back against Fouchier (2 Feb, 9:38 am UK)
sections.heading: 5.4 Rambaut pushes back against Fouchier (2 Feb, 9:38 am UK)
sections.summary: Rambaut also pushes back on Fouchier, arguing a non-natural origin could complicate containment and so needs urgent evaluation, not avoidance.

sections.title: Farrar shares his roadmap (2 Feb, 9:48 am UK)
sections.heading: 5.5 Farrar shares his roadmap (2 Feb, 9:48 am UK)
sections.summary: Farrar effectively closes the internal debate, telling the group discussions should pause until the question moves to the WHO — without revealing that HHS had already settled on that plan.

sections.title: In parallel: discussion on Slack
sections.heading: 5.6 In parallel: discussion on Slack
sections.summary: On Slack, Andersen and Rambaut privately dismiss Fouchier and Drosten as ‘too conflicted to think about this issue straight’, agree to route around them going forward, and settle on writing the eventual report ‘erring on the side of extreme caution’ toward a natural-origin conclusion.

sections.title: Farrar shares the passaging hypothesis with the ‘Bethesda boys’
sections.heading: 6. Farrar shares the passaging hypothesis with the ‘Bethesda boys’
sections.summary: Sets up Farrar's follow-up push to Fauci and Collins, introducing passaging as the more realistic non-natural hypothesis after the call's clash.

sections.title: Collins gets back to Farrar, partly paraphrasing Fouchier (2 Feb, 5:27 am EST)
sections.heading: 6.1 Collins gets back to Farrar, partly paraphrasing Fouchier (2 Feb, 5:27 am EST)
sections.summary: Collins tells Farrar he's leaning toward a natural origin, echoing some of Fouchier's and Drosten's call-room arguments.

sections.title: Farrar updates the ‘Bethesda boys’ with the passaging hypothesis (2 Feb, noon UK, 6:53 am EST)
sections.heading: 6.2 Farrar updates the ‘Bethesda boys’ with the passaging hypothesis (2 Feb, noon UK, 6:53 am EST)
sections.summary: Farrar reintroduces passaging (which Fouchier and Drosten hadn't actually addressed) and makes a prescient call: he's honestly at 50:50, and it will likely ‘remain grey’ unless there's access to the Wuhan lab.

sections.title: Fauci and Collins reply to Farrar (2 Feb, 7:03am & 10:30am EST)
sections.heading: 6.3 Fauci and Collins reply to Farrar (2 Feb, 7:03am & 10:30am EST)
sections.summary: Collins notes the passaging possibility and suggests Wellcome itself could pick up the question if the WHO is too slow; Fauci confirms waiting is not acceptable.

sections.title: In Parallel: Trying to get the WHO on-board
sections.heading: 7. In Parallel: Trying to get the WHO on-board
sections.summary: Sets up the parallel diplomatic push to get the WHO to formally take over the origin question.

sections.title: Farrar and Collins join forces to try to convince the WHO to pick up the origin question (1–2 Feb)
sections.heading: 7.1 Farrar and Collins join forces to try to convince the WHO to pick up the origin question (1–2 Feb)
sections.summary: Farrar struggles to reach Tedros or his chief of staff Schwartländer — a former WHO China representative — to get the broader WHO process moving.

sections.title: Farrar’s call with WHO — The ‘Tedros Proposal’ (2 Feb, ~ 5 pm UK)
sections.heading: 7.2 Farrar’s call with WHO — The ‘Tedros Proposal’ (2 Feb, ~ 5 pm UK)
sections.summary: Farrar, Schwartländer and Ryan agree to ask Tedros to take over a forensic investigation of the origin — the email explicitly frames this as getting ‘ahead of the science and the narrative’, which Fauci and Collins also worry the WHO will be too slow to deliver on.

sections.title: Farrar’s call with China’s ex Minister of Health Chen Zhu (2 Feb)
sections.heading: 7.3 Farrar’s call with China’s ex Minister of Health Chen Zhu (2 Feb)

evidence.raw: _Spike_). The purpose of the call was to let the Chinese Government know, via a back channel, that some enquiries in the origin of the outbreak were likely, and that it would be essential to keep open links with China even if a non-natural origin was the conclusion.

sections.summary: Farrar calls former Chinese health minister Chen Zhu as a back-channel, to warn Beijing that an origin inquiry is coming and to keep communication open regardless of the outcome.

sections.title: Grigsby contacts the WHO (2–3 Feb)
sections.heading: 7.4 Grigsby contacts the WHO (2–3 Feb)
sections.summary: HHS's Grigsby forwards the ‘Tedros Proposal’ document to the WHO's US liaison office, with State Department officials copied in.

sections.summary: Sets up a parallel US ‘Track II’ diplomatic channel, run through the National Academies (NASEM) and China's CAS, to get isolates and data out of China.

sections.title: Introduction: Track II diplomacy, NASEM and CAS
sections.heading: 8.1 Introduction: Track II diplomacy, NASEM and CAS
sections.summary: Introduces NASEM's Track II science-diplomacy channel with China's CAS (led by LeDuc and Franz), already in use before the outbreak and which would shape the choices made around the Farrar call.

sections.title: Isolates Effort #1: NASEM to CAS (starting ~17 Jan)
sections.heading: 8.2 Isolates Effort #1: NASEM to CAS (starting ~17 Jan)
sections.summary: LeDuc flatters Chinese counterparts in a published Op-Ed while quietly asking for virus isolates; NASEM leadership formally backs the request, and by early February CAS's president signals the WIV is willing to share.

sections.title: Isolates effort #2: OSTP (White House) — NASEM — CAS (from 3 Feb)
sections.heading: 8.3 Isolates effort #2: OSTP (White House) — NASEM — CAS (from 3 Feb)

sections.summary: A White House-backed request to NASEM for data/isolates turns, at a 3 Feb expert meeting including Andersen, Daszak, Fauci and Baric, into a drafting fight over origin wording — Andersen reports Baric attacking him on the call as pushing ‘crackpot theories’ — ending with the final NASEM letter dodging the origin question entirely.

sections.title: Some problematic reporting, courtesy of Fauci (6 Feb)
sections.heading: 8.4 Some problematic reporting, courtesy of Fauci (6 Feb)

sections.summary: An ABC article misrepresents the NASEM exercise and quotes Fauci sounding confident the US could tell if the virus were lab-made — alarming China just as Chen Zhu's back-channel outreach was underway, and later fuelling Daszak's resentment of Andersen.

sections.title: Rumours of a parallel US intel investigation spread (8–9 Feb)
sections.heading: 8.5 Rumours of a parallel US intel investigation spread (8–9 Feb)
sections.summary: LeDuc tells NASEM's Hamburg an accidental release from the WIV's BSL-3 (though not its BSL-4) work is plausible, then hours later tells intelligence contacts an accidental release is ‘highly unlikely’.

sections.title: LeDuc sends some pointed questions to Yuan Zhiming of the WIV (9 Feb)
sections.heading: 8.6 LeDuc sends some pointed questions to Yuan Zhiming of the WIV (9 Feb)
sections.summary: The same day, LeDuc presses the WIV's Yuan Zhiming to ‘fess up’ to any biosafety shortcomings — again at odds with what he'd just told US intelligence about the risk being low.

sections.title: Track II hits a wall with the isolates request (10 Feb)
sections.heading: 8.7 Track II hits a wall with the isolates request (10 Feb)
sections.summary: The OSTP/NASEM effort ends in fiasco: the public misreads it as an origin investigation, and China draws the opposite conclusion from Fauci's comments to the real ask for isolates.

sections.title: All roads now lead to the WHO (11–13 Feb)
sections.heading: 8.8 All roads now lead to the WHO (11–13 Feb)
sections.summary: China tells NASEM that isolate-sharing must now go through a WHO framework — leaving the US Track II effort, in LeDuc's own words, unimpressed by the WHO's ability to deliver.

sections.summary: Andersen's first one-page draft (1 Feb) flags the BamHI site and the furin cleavage site as the two potentially problematic features, discarding direct gene editing in favour of tissue-culture passage as the leading non-natural hypothesis.

sections.heading: 9.2 Garry is added — conversations run free (2 Feb)
sections.summary: Garry joins the drafting Slack and Google Doc.

sections.heading: 9.3 Some are excluded (2 Feb)

sections.summary: Sets up the moment the draft report is first shared outside the core group, with Fauci and Collins.

sections.heading: 10.1 Fist sent: Rough draft (4 Feb, morning UK)
sections.summary: Andersen and Holmes finish a four-page draft ruling out deliberate engineering but leaving passaging open; Holmes shares it with Farrar (and from there Fauci and Collins) before Garry — asleep in the US — has even seen it.

sections.heading: 10.2 Second sent: Revised draft (4 Feb, evening UK)

sections.heading: 10.3 Farrar updates Fauci and Collins about the glycans (5 Feb, 6:57 am UK)

sections.heading: 10.4 Pangolins data starts coming in (5 Feb, ~10 am UK)

sections.heading: 10.5 The importance of Fouchier’s and Farzan’s data (5 Feb, afternoon)
sections.summary: The co-authors push to get hold of Farzan's and Fouchier's alluded-to lab data showing passaging can produce a furin site in a coronavirus — data that, tellingly, never surfaces in any P.O. draft or the final paper.

sections.heading: 23.4 Sharing the news with Farrar, Fauci, and Collins (6 Mar)

sections.heading: 23.6 Publication in Nature Medicine (17 Mar, < 3pm EST)

sections.heading: 23.7 The NIAID Office of Communications is informed (17 Mar, 3:01 pm EST)

sections.heading: 24.1 Trump shows little interest in the origin question (to 12 Mar)
sections.summary: Through early March, Trump stays conciliatory toward China while chasing a trade deal, criticised at the time only for downplaying the pandemic's risk — not for blaming China for it.

sections.title: Pompeo gets frustrated by China’s lack of transparency (6 Mar)
sections.heading: 24.2 Pompeo gets frustrated by China’s lack of transparency (6 Mar)
sections.summary: As the trade deal fades and tensions rise, Pompeo calls it ‘incredibly frustrating’ to get data from China and uses the term ‘Wuhan virus’ on 6 Mar — a complaint the piece judges factually correct, if not widely recognised as such at the time.

sections.heading: 24.3 China wolf-warrior Lijian Zhao blames the US (12–13 Mar)

sections.title: Trump starts slowly shifting (16–17 Mar)
sections.heading: 24.5 Trump starts slowly shifting (16–17 Mar)
sections.summary: On the evening of 16 Mar, Trump tweets about the ‘Chinese virus’ for the first time, explaining it as a response to China's own false claim that the US military had brought the virus there.

sections.heading: 24.6 A chorus of condemnations (from 17 Mar)
sections.summary: China reacts angrily and expels NYT, WSJ and Washington Post journalists on 17 Mar, the same day US media frame Trump's tweet as straightforward racism — and P.O. is published.

sections.title: Confusion in the Conclusions
sections.heading: 25.2 Confusion in the Conclusions
sections.summary: The paper's single most-cited sentence is shown to be logically vacuous: finding ‘all notable features’ in nature elsewhere is equally consistent with either a natural origin or a lab-engineered one built from those same natural parts.

sections.title: Confusion in the Approach
sections.heading: 25.3 Confusion in the Approach
sections.summary: The paper's ‘parsimony’ claim for a natural RBD is exposed as comparing the wrong kind of odds — generic background probability instead of the actual circumstances (timing, location, known research) of the outbreak.

sections.heading: 26.7 Altmetric High and political considerations (end of April)
sections.summary: The co-authors return to celebrating the paper's renewed Altmetric score, even as Andersen takes an unexpectedly political stance on a White House advisory call.

sections.title: Recap: How did we end up there?
sections.heading: 26.8 Recap: How did we end up there?
sections.summary: A reflective recap: the co-authors, cornered between the WHO's need for access and the NIH's preferred narrative, quietly set a much higher bar of proof for a lab origin than for a natural one — the asymmetry the piece says explains the whole drafting process.
